absorbed-dose.definition: The amount of radiation energy absorbed by matter, measured in gray (Gy). It represents the energy deposited per unit mass of tissue or material.

alpha-particle.definition: A heavy particle consisting of 2 protons and 2 neutrons (identical to a helium-4 nucleus) emitted during radioactive decay. Has low penetrating power but high ionizing ability.
quickFacts: Stopped by a sheet of paper
Emitted by heavy elements like uranium

atom.definition: The smallest unit of matter that retains the properties of an element. Consists of a nucleus (protons and neutrons) surrounded by electrons.

atomic-number.definition: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom. This number defines the chemical element and its position in the periodic table.

background-radiation.definition: Natural environmental radiation present everywhere from cosmic rays, radon gas, radioactive materials in the Earth's crust, and even in our bodies.
background-radiation.debunkingSnippet: All radiation is not man-made. Natural background radiation accounts for the majority of human radiation exposure.

sources.title: Sources and Effects of Ionizing Radiation

becquerel.definition: The SI unit of radioactivity, equal to one nuclear decay per second. Named after Henri Becquerel who discovered radioactivity.
quickFacts: Used to measure activity of radioactive sources

beta-particle.definition: A high-speed electron or positron emitted during radioactive beta decay. More penetrating than alpha particles but less than gamma rays.
quickFacts: Stopped by aluminum foil or plastic

binding-energy.definition: The energy required to disassemble a nucleus into its component protons and neutrons. Also the energy released when a nucleus forms.
quickFacts: Iron-56 has highest binding energy per nucleon

chain-reaction.definition: A self-sustaining series of nuclear fission events where neutrons released from one fission trigger additional fission reactions.

containment-building.definition: A massive reinforced concrete structure surrounding a nuclear reactor, designed to prevent the release of radioactive materials even during severe accidents.

control-rods.definition: Rods made of neutron-absorbing materials (like boron or cadmium) inserted into a reactor core to control the rate of nuclear fission by absorbing neutrons.
quickFacts: Can start or stop nuclear reactions
Inserted to slow or stop reactions

cosmic-radiation.definition: High-energy radiation from outer space that constantly bombards Earth. A component of background radiation, with exposure increasing at higher altitudes.
quickFacts: Comes from sun and deep space

critical-mass.definition: The minimum amount of fissile material needed to maintain a self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction.

cyclotron.definition: A type of particle accelerator that uses electric and magnetic fields to accelerate charged particles in a spiral path, used to produce medical isotopes.

decay.definition: The process by which unstable atomic nuclei spontaneously emit radiation and transform into more stable nuclei.

defense-in-depth.definition: A nuclear safety philosophy using multiple, independent layers of safety systems to protect against accidents and prevent radiation release.

dose-rate.definition: The amount of radiation dose absorbed per unit time, typically measured in microsieverts per hour (μSv/h) or millisieverts per year (mSv/yr).

dosimeter.definition: A device worn by radiation workers to measure and record the cumulative dose of ionizing radiation received over time.
quickFacts: Various types: film badge, TLD, electronic

electron.definition: A negatively charged subatomic particle that orbits the nucleus of an atom in electron shells or orbitals.
quickFacts: Can be emitted as beta particles

enrichment.definition: The process of increasing the concentration of uranium-235 isotope in uranium. Natural uranium contains only 0.7% U-235; reactor fuel typically needs 3-5%.

exposure.definition: Contact with or absorption of radiation from radioactive materials or radiation-producing devices. Can be external or internal.

nuclear-fission.definition: The process of splitting a heavy atomic nucleus (like uranium-235 or plutonium-239) into two lighter nuclei, releasing energy and neutrons.

nuclear-fusion.definition: The process of combining light atomic nuclei (like hydrogen) to form heavier nuclei, releasing vast amounts of energy. Powers the sun and stars.
quickFacts: Extremely difficult to achieve on Earth

fuel-rods.definition: Long metal tubes containing uranium fuel pellets used in nuclear reactors. Arranged in bundles called fuel assemblies.

gamma-ray.definition: Highly penetrating electromagnetic radiation emitted during radioactive decay. Has no mass or charge and travels at the speed of light.

geiger-counter.definition: A portable instrument that detects and measures ionizing radiation by counting the electrical pulses produced when radiation ionizes gas in a detector tube.

gray.definition: The SI unit of absorbed radiation dose, equal to one joule of radiation energy absorbed per kilogram of matter.

half-life.definition: The time required for half of the atoms in a radioactive sample to decay. Each radioactive isotope has a unique half-life.
quickFacts: Ranges from fractions of seconds to billions of years

heavy-water.definition: Water in which hydrogen atoms are replaced by deuterium (heavy hydrogen). Used as a moderator in some nuclear reactors to slow down neutrons.

hot-cell.definition: A heavily shielded facility for safely handling highly radioactive materials. Workers manipulate materials remotely using mechanical arms.

ionizing-radiation.definition: High-energy radiation capable of removing electrons from atoms, creating ions. Includes alpha particles, beta particles, gamma rays, X-rays, and neutrons.

isotope.definition: Atoms of the same element (same number of protons) with different numbers of neutrons. Some isotopes are stable, others are radioactive.

ion-chamber.definition: A radiation detection device that measures dose rates by collecting the electrical charge produced when radiation ionizes gas between two electrodes.

linear-accelerator.definition: A machine that accelerates charged particles in a straight line using electromagnetic waves. Used for radiotherapy and particle physics research.

low-level-waste.definition: Radioactive waste with relatively low levels of radioactivity. Includes contaminated protective clothing, tools, filters, and medical waste.
quickFacts: About 90% of nuclear waste by volume

moderator.definition: A material (such as water, heavy water, or graphite) used in nuclear reactors to slow down fast neutrons, making them more likely to cause fission.

meltdown.definition: A severe nuclear reactor accident where the reactor core overheats and fuel melts due to loss of cooling. Extremely rare with modern safety systems.
quickFacts: Modern reactors have passive safety features

mass-defect.definition: The difference between the mass of an atomic nucleus and the sum of the masses of its individual protons and neutrons. This 'missing' mass is converted to binding energy.

neutron.definition: A neutral subatomic particle found in the nucleus of atoms. Has approximately the same mass as a proton but carries no electrical charge.

nuclear-reactor.definition: A device that initiates and controls a sustained nuclear chain reaction. Used primarily for generating electricity, but also for research and isotope production.
quickFacts: Cannot explode like a nuclear bomb
nuclear-reactor.debunkingSnippet: Nuclear reactors cannot explode like atomic bombs due to different fuel enrichment levels and design principles.

nucleus.definition: The central core of an atom, containing protons and neutrons. Contains 99.9% of the atom's mass but occupies only a tiny fraction of its volume.
quickFacts: Held together by strong nuclear force

proton.definition: A positively charged subatomic particle found in the nucleus of atoms. The number of protons determines the element's identity.

plutonium-239.definition: A fissile isotope of plutonium used in nuclear reactors and weapons. Produced in reactors when uranium-238 captures neutrons.

radiation.definition: Energy emitted as particles or electromagnetic waves. Can be ionizing (high energy, can damage cells) or non-ionizing (lower energy).

sources.title: Sources and Effects of Ionizing Radiation

radionuclide.definition: An unstable isotope that undergoes radioactive decay, emitting radiation. Also called radioactive isotope or radioisotope.

radon.definition: A naturally occurring radioactive gas produced by the decay of uranium in soil and rocks. The largest source of natural radiation exposure for most people.
quickFacts: Second leading cause of lung cancer

reactor-core.definition: The central part of a nuclear reactor containing the fuel assemblies where fission reactions occur and heat is generated.

roentgen.definition: An older unit of radiation exposure measuring ionization in air. Named after Wilhelm Roentgen who discovered X-rays. Largely replaced by SI units.

sievert.definition: The SI unit of equivalent radiation dose, measuring the biological effect of ionizing radiation on humans. Takes into account the type of radiation and tissue sensitivity.

shielding.definition: Barriers made of dense materials (lead, concrete, water) that reduce or block radiation exposure by absorbing or deflecting radiation.

scintillation-detector.definition: A device that detects radiation by converting the energy deposited by radiation into visible light flashes, which are then measured by photomultipliers.

spent-fuel.definition: Nuclear fuel that has been used in a reactor and removed because it can no longer efficiently sustain fission. Still highly radioactive.
quickFacts: Stored in pools or dry casks

thermal-neutron.definition: A slow-moving neutron in thermal equilibrium with its surroundings. These neutrons are ideal for causing fission in uranium-235.

transmutation.definition: The conversion of one chemical element into another through nuclear reactions or radioactive decay.

tritium.definition: A radioactive isotope of hydrogen with one proton and two neutrons. Used in fusion research, luminous devices, and as a tracer.

uranium-235.definition: A fissile isotope of uranium that can sustain a nuclear chain reaction. Makes up about 0.7% of natural uranium. Used as nuclear fuel.

uranium-238.definition: The most abundant isotope of uranium (99.3% of natural uranium). Not fissile but can be converted to fissile plutonium-239.

uranium-hexafluoride.definition: A chemical compound used in the uranium enrichment process. It can exist as a solid, liquid, or gas, making it useful for separation processes.

vitrification.definition: The process of turning high-level nuclear waste into a stable glass form for long-term storage. The waste is immobilized in a glass matrix.

radioactive-waste.definition: Radioactive by-products from nuclear power generation, medical applications, and research that require safe management and disposal.

watt.definition: The SI unit of power, measuring the rate of energy transfer. Nuclear power plants are rated in megawatts (MW) or gigawatts (GW).

x-ray.definition: High-energy electromagnetic radiation produced when high-speed electrons strike matter. Used extensively in medical imaging and security.

yellowcake.definition: A concentrated uranium ore product (uranium oxide) obtained after mining and milling. Named for its yellow color, though it can also be brown or black.

yield.definition: The amount of energy released by a nuclear explosion, typically measured in tons or megatons of TNT equivalent.

z-number.definition: Another term for atomic number - the number of protons in an atom's nucleus, which determines the element's identity.

zero-power-reactor.definition: A nuclear reactor that operates at very low power levels (typically less than 1 watt), used for research, training, and testing without producing significant heat.
